chunks: Muhammad ibn Muslim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the water in which animals urinate, dogs lap, and the one in a state of major ritual impurity (janabah) bathes. He said: When the water is of the measure of a kurr, nothing will make it impure.

key_terms.الدَّوَابّ: al-dawabb: riding animals, livestock, or beasts of burden; broadly refers to four-legged animals
key_terms.الْجُنُب: al-junub: a person in the state of janabah (major ritual impurity), requiring a full ritual bath (ghusl) before performing prayer
key_terms.طَهَارَة: tahara: ritual purity; the prerequisite state for valid prayer and other acts of worship
key_terms.كُرّ: kurr: an Islamic unit of water volume equal to approximately 384 litres (or a cube ~42.87cm per side); water reaching this threshold is considered 'kurr water' and is not made impure by contact with impurities
key_terms.يُنَجِّسْهُ: yunajjishu: to make ritually impure, to defile; from najasa (ritual impurity)

ai.seo_question: What volume of water cannot be made ritually impure according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes one of the foundational principles of Islamic ritual purity law (tahara): water reaching the volume of a kurr (approximately 384 litres, or a cube roughly 3.5 hand-spans per side) cannot be rendered ritually impure (najis) by contact with impure substances. Muhammad ibn Muslim, one of the most trusted companions of Imam al-Sadiq, reports this ruling directly from the Imam. In the early Islamic community, questions about water purity were critical for enabling daily acts of worship such as wudu and ghusl, and this hadith provided clear legal boundaries distinguishing small, easily-contaminated water from large, self-purifying bodies.
word_analysis: the one in a state of major ritual impurity (janabah)
a kurr (Islamic unit of water volume, approx. 384 litres)
